strengths: BrepCoder addresses a relevant problem in geometric understanding: recovering editable CAD programs and supporting downstream tasks directly from industry-standard B-rep inputs. Aligning geometry with procedural code is a sensible foundation for this goal.

The strongest evidence is the reverse-engineering comparison in Table 1: median Chamfer distance improves from CADCL’s 0.972 to 0.499 (×10⁻³), while parameter accuracy increases from 81.52% to 81.93%. This supports improved geometric reconstruction despite slightly lower command accuracy.

The evaluation covers four tasks, and Table 3 investigates alignment objectives, encoder freezing, model size, projector depth, and reverse-engineering pretraining. The CoCa-versus-CLIP comparison provides useful evidence for including a generative alignment objective.

The discussion of modeling ambiguity is valuable. Figure 5 illustrates why geometrically equivalent programs can receive low sequence accuracy, appropriately qualifying the interpretation of command-based metrics.
The 1.5B model achieves competitive CAD-QA accuracy of 79%, compared with 81% for PointLLM-7B. The manuscript also clearly attributes its principal building blocks to UV-Net, CoCa, and CAD-Llama.
weaknesses: The downstream comparisons do not isolate the proposed method’s contribution. Completion provides BrepCoder with the target B-rep while CAD-Llama receives textual descriptions; error correction compares complete B-rep geometry against single rendered images. The ReCAD comparison additionally uses a different dataset and programming language. These results demonstrate benefits of richer input but cannot establish the claimed methodological superiority. Matched-input baselines are needed.

Because completion and correction receive the complete target geometry, the model could largely solve them by regenerating a program from the B-rep. There is no comparison against simply applying the reverse-engineering model, or removing the partial/corrupted code. Consequently, the experiments do not establish whether the model uses the supplied program or acquires distinct editing capabilities.

The central claims of unified multitask operation and strong generalization are insufficiently substantiated. Section 3.2 does not clearly specify whether Stage 2 produces one jointly trained checkpoint or separate task-specific models, and no task mixture or post-adaptation reverse-engineering results are reported. Evaluation uses supervised downstream adaptation and in-distribution splits, without testing unseen task transfer or broader CAD distributions.

The evidence for the two-stage strategy is mixed. In Table 3(b), completion parameter accuracy changes only from 87.91% to 87.94%; correction command accuracy and invalid ratio worsen, although Chamfer distance improves from 0.405 to 0.335. The QA increase from 71% to 79% is encouraging, but uncertainty estimates and an explicit question count are absent. These findings do not justify attributing broad gains to acquired design logic.

Reproducibility and metric comparability require substantial clarification. Training schedules, optimizer settings, batch sizes, fine-tuning configuration, decoding settings, parameter tolerance, and precise corruption distributions are missing. Table 1 reports baseline invalid ratios such as 13.98 alongside BrepCoder’s 0.009 without specifying percentage-versus-fraction conventions. It is also unclear whether all reconstruction baselines use identical splits and evaluation code. Completion command accuracy differs between Tables 2 and 3 (92.69 versus 92.96).

The alignment decoder description is technically ambiguous: Section 3.1 states that generation queries use the global EOS representation of the CAD code, whereas Eq. (4) defines causal prediction conditioned only on preceding tokens. The masking and token-level decoder inputs need clarification to establish that the captioning objective cannot access future target information.

Assessed as Algorithms/General, the originality primarily lies in integrating established components. Such integration can be valuable, but stronger controlled evidence is necessary here: the promising reconstruction result does not resolve the comparison, task-definition, and reproducibility concerns underlying the broader contribution.

strengths: BrepCoder addresses a relevant CAD understanding problem: connecting native B-rep geometry to editable modeling code and supporting several tasks through a common architecture. The integration of UV-Net, CoCa alignment, and an LLM is coherent, and the main inherited components are appropriately acknowledged.

The strongest evidence is reverse engineering on DeepCAD: Table 1 reports median Chamfer distance of 0.499 versus CADCL's 0.972, approximately a 49% reduction, with slightly higher parameter accuracy. These results suggest useful geometric reconstruction capabilities.

The CoCa-versus-CLIP ablation supports the value of generative alignment, while CAD-QA achieves competitive reported accuracy with a 1.5B backbone. Figure 5 also usefully explains why equivalent CAD constructions can receive low sequence accuracy.

Completion supplies BrepCoder with target B-rep geometry while CAD-Llama receives textual descriptions; error correction compares complete B-rep inputs against single images. ReCAD additionally uses a different dataset and programming language, so its Chamfer distance cannot establish comparative superiority. Matched-input baselines are needed.

Because completion and correction receive the target geometry, a key missing baseline is simply reconstructing code from that B-rep using the Stage 1 model. Without this comparison or ablations removing the partial/corrupted code, the experiments do not establish that BrepCoder uses those inputs meaningfully rather than solving reverse engineering again.

The evidence for the central staged-training claim is mixed. In Table 3(b), completion parameter accuracy changes only from 87.91 to 87.94; correction command accuracy and invalid ratio worsen, although correction Chamfer distance and CAD-QA improve. Without repeated runs or uncertainty estimates, these results do not support the broad claim that Stage 1 consistently imparts transferable design logic.

The unified-model claim remains insufficiently documented. Section 3.2 does not specify whether Stage 2 produces one jointly trained checkpoint or separate task-specific models, nor provide task mixing details or reverse-engineering performance after adaptation. The reported supervised evaluations also do not establish generalization to unseen tasks or substantially different CAD distributions.

Reproducibility and metric interpretation have important gaps. Training schedules, optimizer settings, fine-tuning configuration, decoding settings, parameter tolerance, and corruption distributions are unspecified. Table 1 reports baseline invalid ratios above 1 alongside BrepCoder's 0.009 without clarifying percentage-versus-fraction units. Chamfer normalization and handling of invalid outputs also need specification, particularly for cross-dataset comparisons.

The alignment description is technically ambiguous: Section 3.1 says the multimodal decoder queries with the full-code EOS embedding, whereas Equation 4 describes causal generation conditioned on preceding tokens. Decoder inputs and attention masks must be clarified to rule out access to future target information. Under the default Algorithms/General assessment, the largely established components could still support acceptance through convincing empirical evidence, but the unresolved evaluation and methodological issues currently outweigh the promising reconstruction results.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: connecting native B-rep geometry to editable CAD programs and downstream reasoning. Supporting several CAD tasks through a common architecture is a useful direction for computer vision and engineering automation.

The strongest evidence is the reverse-engineering result in Table 1. BrepCoder reports a median Chamfer distance of 0.499 versus CADCL's 0.972, approximately a 49% reduction, while slightly improving parameter accuracy from 81.52% to 81.93%. The comparison against another B-rep method is particularly relevant.

The discussion of modeling ambiguity is valuable. Figure 5 illustrates why different valid construction histories can produce equivalent geometry, appropriately qualifying the interpretation of command accuracy.

The ablations provide useful evidence for individual design choices: CoCa alignment improves geometric reconstruction over CLIP, and Stage 1 improves CAD-QA accuracy from 71% to 79%. Achieving 79% with a 1.5B backbone, compared with PointLLM's reported 81%, is encouraging.
weaknesses: The downstream comparisons do not isolate the proposed method's contribution. Completion provides BrepCoder with the target B-rep but CAD-Llama with a textual description; error correction compares complete geometry against single images. These experiments demonstrate the benefit of richer input but cannot establish architectural or training superiority. ReCAD additionally uses a different dataset and programming language, so its Chamfer distance is not a controlled comparison. Matched-input baselines are needed.

The central claim of a unified multi-task model remains insufficiently demonstrated. Section 3.2 does not clearly establish whether Stage 2 jointly trains one checkpoint or produces separate task-specific checkpoints, and provides no task-mixture schedule or post-adaptation reverse-engineering results. Because completion and correction receive the complete target geometry, a reconstruction-only baseline that ignores the supplied partial or erroneous program is also important to establish task-specific reasoning.

Evidence for broadly transferable 'design logic' is mixed. In Table 3(b), Stage 1 changes completion parameter accuracy only from 87.91% to 87.94%; for correction, command accuracy and invalid ratio worsen, although Chamfer distance improves. The CAD-QA improvement is promising, but uncertainty estimates are absent for the small benchmark. These results support narrower claims than strong generalization across complex engineering tasks, particularly without evaluation on unseen CAD distributions or operations.

Reproducibility and metric comparability require substantial clarification. Training schedules, optimization settings, batch sizes, fine-tuning configuration, decoding settings, parameter-noise distributions, and the numerical tolerance used for parameter accuracy are missing. Table 1 reports baseline invalid ratios above 1 alongside BrepCoder's 0.009 without identifying percentage versus fraction units. Chamfer scaling in subsequent tables and treatment of invalid generations are unclear. Completion command accuracy also differs between Tables 2 and 3. These issues affect interpretation of the headline gains.

The alignment description contains a consequential ambiguity: Section 3.1 states that the multimodal decoder uses the global code EOS embedding as its query, whereas Equation 4 describes causal next-token prediction conditioned on preceding tokens. The decoder inputs and attention masks must be specified to establish how token sequences are generated and whether future target information is excluded during captioning training.

Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, originality is primarily the integration of existing UV-Net, CoCa, CAD-Llama code representation, and an LLM projector with staged fine-tuning. This integration could merit acceptance with convincing controlled evidence, but the current comparisons and incomplete training specification do not sufficiently establish its incremental value. Overall, the promising reconstruction results are outweighed by unresolved concerns about the central multi-task claims and experimental validity.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in 3D computer vision and CAD: recovering editable modeling programs directly from B-rep geometry. Integrating native geometric features with code generation has practical value. I assess the submission as Algorithms/General.

The reverse-engineering results are compelling on the reported benchmark. Table 1 reduces median Chamfer Distance from CADCL's 0.972 to 0.464 × 10^-3 and invalid ratio from 13.98% to 0.86%, while maintaining competitive command and parameter accuracy.

The framework supports several useful applications, with strong completion and correction results against adapted B-rep baselines. CAD-QA accuracy of 79% is competitive with the reported larger point-cloud models, although it does not establish superiority.

The ablations cover alignment, encoder choice, backbone, freezing, and projector depth. The substantial degradation without Phase 1 supports explicit geometric-code alignment. The discussion and visual examples of nonunique modeling histories appropriately explain why command accuracy alone is insufficient.
The principal components and datasets are attributed, and the supplement provides useful training configurations, hardware details, and additional qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The central claim of a unified multitask model is not adequately established. Section 3.2 and Appendix A.2 describe task-dependent fine-tuning schedules and checkpoint selection, but do not clearly establish that one final checkpoint performs all four tasks. There is no joint-task evaluation or assessment of retention after adaptation. A shared architecture with separate task-specific checkpoints would support a narrower contribution than the general-purpose agent framing.

Completion and correction both receive the target B-rep, from which the complete program can already be reconstructed. The experiments do not isolate whether the model meaningfully uses the partial or erroneous code rather than regenerating from geometry. A B-rep-only reconstruction baseline on these tasks, together with measurements of prefix preservation or preservation of correct code, would substantiate the claimed task-specific reasoning.

Evidence for Stage 1 transfer is mixed. In Table 3(b), completion parameter accuracy changes only from 87.91% to 87.94%; correction command accuracy decreases, although correction CD improves from 0.405 to 0.335. Completion CD and invalid ratio are omitted. The CAD-QA improvement from 71% to 79% is promising, but uncertainty and the exact number of evaluated questions are unreported. These results do not yet justify broad claims of strong generalization through acquired design logic.

Several comparisons cannot isolate methodological gains. CAD-Llama receives textual geometry descriptions, whereas BrepCoder receives precise B-reps; commercial correction models receive one rendered image; and ReCAD is evaluated on a different dataset. The manuscript acknowledges some differences, but still draws superiority conclusions from them. The adapted B-rep baselines are useful, yet a comparably trained code-generating LLM with simpler B-rep alignment would better establish the contribution beyond combining UV-Net, CoCa, and an existing CAD code representation.

The Phase 1 captioning description is technically ambiguous. Section 3.1 says the multimodal decoder uses the global EOS code embedding as its query, whereas Equation (4) specifies autoregressive prediction conditioned on preceding tokens. The decoder inputs and causal masks need clarification: conditioning on an embedding of the complete target code could expose future-token information during alignment.

Evaluation and reproducibility details remain incomplete: the parameter tolerance is unspecified, handling of unequal sequence lengths and invalid outputs in CD is unclear, and the corruption noise distribution is not defined. Broad industrial applicability is supported primarily by DeepCAD-derived generation tasks, without evaluation beyond its modeling vocabulary or on real correction errors. Separately, completion command accuracy is inconsistently reported as 92.69 in Table 2 and 92.96 in Table 3; this appears to be a correctable reporting issue.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem in geometric understanding: connecting industry-standard B-rep geometry to editable CAD programs and downstream language tasks. Direct B-rep conditioning has clear practical value.

The reported reverse-engineering results are strong. Table 1 reduces median Chamfer Distance from CADCL's 0.972 to 0.464 × 10⁻³ and invalidity from 13.98% to 0.86%. Improvements over B-rep-conditioned baselines on completion and correction provide additional evidence beyond comparisons with weaker input modalities.

The ablations meaningfully investigate alignment, encoder choice, freezing, backbone, and projector depth. The CoCa-versus-CLIP comparison supports combining generative and contrastive alignment. The supplement provides useful training configurations.

The discussion of nonunique CAD histories appropriately explains why command accuracy alone can penalize geometrically valid reconstructions. CAD-QA accuracy of 79% is also competitive with the evaluated larger models, although not the best result.
weaknesses: The central unified multitask claim is not adequately established. Section 3.2 and Appendix A.2 describe downstream fine-tuning with task-specific schedules, but do not clearly establish whether one final checkpoint performs all four tasks. There is no joint-task evaluation, retention analysis, or evidence of mutual knowledge sharing. A reusable architecture with separately fine-tuned models is useful, but supports a narrower claim.

Evidence for Stage 1 acquiring broadly transferable design logic is mixed. In Table 3(b), completion parameter accuracy changes only from 87.91 to 87.94, while correction command accuracy decreases from 99.43 to 99.08. Correction geometry and CAD-QA do improve, but completion geometry/validity ablations and uncertainty estimates are absent. The completion command score also differs between Tables 2 and 3: 92.69 versus 92.96.

Completion and correction receive the complete target B-rep, so they can potentially be solved by reconstructing the target while disregarding the supplied partial or erroneous program. The paper does not compare against Stage 1 reconstruction on these same examples or ablate the code input. Consequently, the results do not establish how much the model actually completes or repairs an existing design, preserves its valid history, or reasons about errors.

Several comparisons cannot isolate methodological improvements. CAD-Llama receives textual descriptions, whereas commercial correction models receive a single rendered view; both provide less geometric information than B-rep. The claim of superiority over ReCAD is particularly unsupported because its result comes from a different dataset. The B-rep baselines help, but their adaptation and training details are insufficiently specified, and the closest B-rep MLLM, BrepLLM, is not experimentally compared.

Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, methodological originality is modest: the framework combines attributed UV-Net, CoCa, CAD-Llama's representation, and standard projector-based LLM adaptation. Such integration can warrant acceptance, but the general-purpose engineering-reasoning claims exceed evaluation on DeepCAD-derived reconstruction/corruption tasks and a small CAD-QA split. No held-out operation, distribution-shift, or real editing-error evaluation substantiates broader generalization.

Some technical details require clarification for reproducibility. Section 3.1 describes the captioning decoder query as the full-code EOS embedding, whereas Eq. (4) specifies autoregressive prefix conditioning; the actual token flow and causal masking need clarification. The parameter tolerance, corruption-noise distribution, treatment of invalid outputs in Chamfer evaluation, and decoding settings are also unspecified. These gaps weaken confidence in an otherwise promising empirical contribution.

strengths: BrepCoder addresses a practically relevant problem: connecting native B-rep geometry to editable CAD programs and downstream language-based tasks. The integration of geometric encoding, code alignment, and an LLM is coherent and relevant to computer vision for engineering.

The strongest evidence is the reverse-engineering result in Table 1: median Chamfer Distance improves from CADCL’s 0.972 to 0.464, while the invalid ratio falls from 13.98% to 0.86%. These are meaningful improvements in geometric fidelity and executable output, despite slightly lower command accuracy.

Completion and error correction also improve over the adapted B-rep baselines. The 79% CAD-QA accuracy is competitive with substantially larger point-cloud models; achieving the highest score is unnecessary for this result to be useful.

The ablations cover alignment, encoder choice, freezing, backbone size, and projector depth. Supplementary training configurations and qualitative examples help document the approach, and the principal reused methods are explicitly attributed.
The discussion of modeling ambiguity is valuable: different valid construction histories can produce equivalent geometry, so command agreement alone can underestimate reconstruction quality.
weaknesses: The central unified-model claim is not adequately established. Section 3.2 and Appendix A.2 describe task-specific fine-tuning schedules and checkpoint selection, but do not clearly demonstrate that one final checkpoint performs all four tasks. Joint training, task mixing, and retention of reverse-engineering ability after adaptation are not evaluated. A reusable architecture is supported more clearly than a single general-purpose CAD agent.

Completion and correction both receive the target B-rep, which already supports reconstruction of the complete program. The experiments do not establish whether BrepCoder meaningfully uses the partial or erroneous code rather than reconstructing from geometry. Evaluating the Stage 1 model directly on these tasks, removing or shuffling the code input, and measuring preservation of supplied correct operations would distinguish task-specific reasoning from reconstruction.

Several comparisons confound model quality with available information. CAD-Llama receives text rather than exact geometry, and GPT/Gemini receive a single image. ReCAD uses a different dataset, so its Chamfer Distance cannot substantiate comparative superiority. The adapted B-rep baselines help, but a matched B-rep-conditioned code LLM without the proposed alignment pipeline would better isolate the contribution.

The evidence for transferable design logic is mixed. In Table 3(b), completion parameter accuracy changes only from 87.91 to 87.94 without versus with Stage 1, and completion geometry and validity are omitted. Correction geometry improves and QA gains eight percentage points, but uncertainty estimates and a training-budget-matched control are absent. DeepCAD reconstruction and synthetic corruption experiments also provide limited support for the broader industrial-generalization claims.

The Phase 1 captioning description contains a consequential ambiguity. Section 3.1 says the multimodal decoder queries with the global EOS code feature, whereas Equation 4 specifies autoregressive conditioning on preceding tokens. The manuscript should clarify token-level decoder inputs and causal masking, since a representation of the complete target code could otherwise expose future-token information during training.

Evaluation reproducibility needs improvement: the parameter tolerance is unspecified, the stated conditional parameter-accuracy metric is unclear about its denominator, and the corruption distribution and treatment of invalid outputs in Chamfer Distance are insufficiently documented. Completion command accuracy also differs between Tables 2 and 3 (92.69 versus 92.96). Overall, the promising reconstruction gains make this a close decision, but the unresolved evidence around the central multi-task contribution favors borderline rejection.
